en.g: a male given name from Old Norse, variant of Eivind

1000476.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse Eyvindr, through a younger Norwegian reduced form, ultimately from Proto-Norse *Auja-winduʀ. The Proto-Norse name is traditionally analysed as containing an element related to *awją (“luck, good fortune”) and the name element *-winduʀ (“victor, victorious lord”), although the precise interpretation of the first element is uncertain.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Even, Swedish Even and Danish Even (“male given name”). See also Eivind and Øyvind.

en.g: a male given name from Hebrew, equivalent to English Jonah
the Book of Jonah, a book of the Old Testament

1001500.etyen:
Derived from Biblical Hebrew יוֹנָה (Yōnā, “dove”), through biblical tradition. The form corresponds more closely to the Hebrew name than Jonas, whose final ⟨s⟩ reflects the Greek and Latin nominative forms. In some cases, the male given name may instead be a short form of Jonatan or Jonathan. Doublet of Jonas (“male given name”).
Compare Danish Jona, Swedish Jona, Finnish Jona and English Jonah (“male given name”).

en.g: a traditional Norwegian dish of crushed flatbread in a soup of meat, peas and grain, with rendered fat

1004828.etyen:
From Setesdal dialect flot (“rendered fat from pork or meat”) + mylje, corresponding to mølje (“dish of flatbread soaked in broth”).
The dialectal first element flot continues Old Norse flot (“floating; fat floating on the surface of a liquid”), related to Old Norse fljóta (“to float”) and Norwegian Bokmål flyte (“to float”). The second element mylje is related to Old Norse mylja (“to crush, crumble”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk flotmølje (“dish of flatbread and rendered fat”).

en.g: devil-may-care, reckless, defiant, uninhibited; boldly unconcerned about consequences or ordinary conventions

i engelsk, fransk, amerikansk, pokkerivoldsk tjeneste ude i verden
in English, French, American, devil-may-care service out in the world

1005084.etyen:
From the expression (gå) pokker i vold (“(to go) to hell”), with -sk (“adjective-forming suffix”).
The expression contains vold (“power, control”), from Old Norse vald (“power, authority”), from Proto-Germanic *waldą (“power, authority”), related to *waldaną (“to rule, wield”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“to rule, be strong”).
